title: A Crimson Nursery
caption: The emission nebula RCW 120, imaged by the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab). Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A crimson cloud glows in this view of RCW 120, also called Sharpless 2-3, an emission nebula and star-forming region in the constellation Scorpius. Dark lanes wind through the red gas.

The red colour comes from ionized hydrogen. Intense heat from young, massive stars inside the nebula energizes the gas, which then gives off light at deep red and infrared wavelengths. The dark lanes are made of the same material but are less energized, so they do not glow.

Emission nebulae often contain bright stars, and such stars build up many heavier elements, silicon and iron among them, by fusing lighter ones together. RCW 120 also shelters an unusual star still in its embryonic stage, which astronomers expect to grow into one of the Milky Way's brightest. The view comes from the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope, which operates at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile.

understand.summary: Taken with the Tek2K camera on the SMARTS 0.9-meter Telescope through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the nebula's light is infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye.
